content: The document outlines a detailed and structured approach to monitoring, evaluating, and improving child health services at healthcare facilities. Continuous Facility Monitoring and Periodic Evaluations 1. Basic Health Screening and Re-examination of Sick Children Regular health screenings are conducted to assess the overall health of children. Sick children are re-examined to ensure proper diagnosis and treatment. 2. Environmental Hygiene and Promotional Materials Observations are made to evaluate the cleanliness of the facility and the availability of health promotion materials. 3. Review of Essential Medicines and Supplies An inventory check is performed to ensure the availability of essential medicines and medical supplies. 4. Review of Policies Supporting Child Health Practices Policies related to child health practices are reviewed to ensure alignment with national and international standards. 5. Review of Sickand Well-Child Registers Registers documenting the care of both sick and well children are reviewed for accuracy and completeness. 6. Review of Staff Coaching for Child Health The training and coaching provided to healthcare staff on child health management are assessed. Development of a Facility Action Plan 1. Using Data to Determine Priority Actions Data collected from facility reviews is analyzed to identify priority actions for a three-month improvement plan. Synthesis of Findings Across Multiple Facilities 1. Synthesis of Facility Review Findings Data from multiple facilities is consolidated into synthesis tables to identify trends and areas for improvement. Monitoring and Evaluation Data for Child Health 1. Completion of Monitoring and Evaluation Tables Data is systematically recorded in tables to track progress and outcomes related to child health services. Annual Implementation Plan for Child Health Improvement 1. Development of an Annual Action Plan Findings from the reviews are used to create an annual implementation plan, linking it to previous plans for continuity. Preparations for Facility Visits 1. Training of External Facilitators External facilitators must be trained in the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) approach and have experience in child assessment, classification, and treatment. They should also have access to the country’s IMCI chart booklet. 2. Authorization for Facility Visits Facilitators must obtain clearance from hospital directors, local health officers, and subnational authorities. A letter of introduction from the Ministry of Health is typically required. 3. Budget Allocation A budget must be secured to cover per diem, transportation, photocopying, and other costs associated with field visits. 4. Identification of Facility Staff One or two staff members from each facility are identified to organize the review, learn the approach, and coordinate the implementation of the facility plan. Periodic Evaluations at District, Subnational, or National Levels 1. Process A team of trained evaluators visits a sample of primary-care facilities, completes checklists, and returns to a central venue to summarize and review data. 2. Participants At least 12 evaluators are required, including members from district, provincial, or national child health departments, facility child health teams, and other health ministry staff or development partners. At least one team member must be trained in IMCI. 3. Timing The process takes six to eight days, including one day for preparation, three to five days for fieldwork, and two days for data analysis and planning. Site Selection for Facility Assessments 1. Option 1: Inclusion of All Facilities All health facilities that have initiated monitoring within the past year are included. Participants may include facility staff, facilitators, and external staff. 2. Option 2: Random Selection At least 18 facilities are randomly selected for national or subnational reviews. This includes a mix of national, provincial, district hospitals, and first-level facilities. Interviews with Caregivers of Sick and Well Children 1. Purpose Caregivers are interviewed to assess the effectiveness of the health system in delivering essential services to infants and young children. 2. Instructions Interviews are conducted in a private setting, and caregivers are selected from clinic registers. Verbal informed consent is obtained, and questions are asked about breastfeeding, complementary feeding, vaccinations, and danger signs. 3. Breastfeeding and Nutrition Questions focus on breastfeeding practices, difficulties, and the introduction of other fluids or foods. The child’s nutritional status is assessed using records or caregiver responses. 4. Vaccinations and Vitamin A The child’s vaccination record is reviewed to determine if all required vaccines have been administered. Questions about vitamin A supplementation and deworming are also included. 5. Danger Signs Caregivers are asked if they recognize danger signs that require immediate medical attention, such as poor feeding, convulsions, or lethargy. Screening, Management, and Prevention of Diarrhea 1. Assessment of Diarrhea Cases Caregivers are asked about the duration and characteristics of the child’s diarrhea. The health worker’s management of the case is reviewed, including the prescription of oral rehydration salts (ORS), zinc, and antibiotics. 2. Counseling and Advice Health workers are evaluated on whether they provided advice on extra fluids, continued feeding, and the use of multivitamins.
